A pipeline that double-counts revenue after a node restart is a system design failure, not a Spark bug. The data engineering design round tests whether you can see that failure coming: whether you ask what one row means, where the data can be replayed from, and which write is allowed to happen twice. This guide gives you a repeatable way to answer that round and the mechanics you need to defend ea

Why the data design round is different
/SystemDesignForDataEngineers/.t: A backend design round asks whether a service stays up and answers fast. A data design round asks whether the numbers are still right after the system has failed, been replayed, and been changed by three teams over a year. /SystemDesignForDataEngineers/.h: Storage: lake, warehouse and lakehouse tables
/SystemDesignForDataEngineers/.t: A plain data lake is a directory of Parquet files: cheap, open, and with no transactions. Two writers can interleave, a reader can see half a job’s output, and an update means rewriting a partition by hand. /SystemDesignForDataEngineers/.h: Hands-on demo: an exactly-once Kafka to Iceberg pipeline
/SystemDesignForDataEngineers/.t: The claim to prove: a replayed micro-batch duplicates rows in an append sink and leaves an idempotent MERGE sink unchanged. The demo also shows two contract rules from step 3: duplicates from producer retries are removed, and a stale event that arrives late does not overwrite newer state.
Replication factor 1 is only because the playground runs one broker.

Run 1 publishes 1,000 orders plus 50 exact copies, the duplicates a producer retry creates when an acknowledgement is lost after the broker stored the write. Run 2 publishes 500 new orders, 30 SHIPPED updates for earlier orders, and 10 PENDING events whose updated_ts is older than the stored PLACED version.

Inside foreachBatch , each micro-batch goes to both sinks. Before the MERGE , a window keeps one row per order_id within the batch, the newest by updated_ts . That step is required, not a nicety: a MERGE whose source has two rows for one target row fails, as the last step shows. The MERGE itself only updates when the incoming version is newer, which is what rejects the stale events.

/SystemDesignForDataEngineers/.t: Partition storage by the column most queries filter on, usually a date or hour of event time, and keep partitions large enough to hold files of hundreds of megabytes. Over-partitioning (by date and user id, say) creates millions of tiny files. Within partitions, sort or cluster by a second frequent filter so file-level min and max statistics can skip files. For skewed joins, Spark’s adaptive query

When consumers fall behind, the log absorbs it, and consumer lag is the signal. Act on it in order: scale the bottleneck stage, bound the batch size so a backlog does not create one enormous batch ( maxOffsetsPerTrigger for Spark’s Kafka source), and shed or defer low-priority work. A backlog larger than retention is data loss, so alert on lag as time (“40 minutes behind”) against the retention wi

/RemoteJobWebsites/.t: Most companies publish openings on their applicant tracking system first, and aggregators pick them up later. Greenhouse, Lever and Ashby host job pages on predictable domains, so you can search them directly: Swap in your own title and add a location, for example (India OR Bengaluru) . In Google, open Tools , then Any time , and choose Past 24 hours or Past week . Two caveats from using this: Sea

Filter by eligible location first. On the global remote boards I checked in one week, almost every data engineering role was limited to the US, Europe or LATAM. Country filters (Remote Rocketship, Himalayas) and per-listing region lines (We Work Remotely) save the most time. Check that the listing is live. /DataModelingForDataEngineers/.h: 1.1 What is data modeling, and why is it important?
/DataModelingForDataEngineers/.t: In plain terms. A data model is the agreement about what each table means, written down before anyone writes a query. A shop receipt shows it well: one receipt per purchase, one printed line per product. Anyone can total the receipt because everyone agrees what a line is. /DataModelingForDataEngineers/.h: 1.2 The three abstraction levels: conceptual, logical, and physical
/DataModelingForDataEngineers/.t: In plain terms. An architect draws a sketch of rooms first, then a floor plan with exact dimensions, then the construction drawings that say which bricks and pipes to use. Data models follow the same three steps. These levels answer different questions. Mixing them makes design reviews argue about implementation before agreeing on the business meaning.

The conceptual model answers which business concepts exist and how they relate . Its artifact is an entity map or a domain model, drawn so a business owner can read it. In the sales example: customers place orders, orders contain lines, and products are sold.

The logical model answers which attributes, keys, constraints, and cardinalities define the model . Its artifact is an ER model, a relational schema, or a dimensional model. In the sales example: one row per order line, with references to the customer, the product, and the date.

The physical model answers how one specific engine stores and reads the model . Its artifacts are DDL, indexes, partitions, files, clustering, and distribution. In the sales example: PostgreSQL B-tree indexes, or Parquet files in an Iceberg table. The same logical model can be implemented as PostgreSQL tables, Spark DataFrames, or Iceberg tables. /DataModelingForDataEngineers/.t: In plain terms. Entities are the nouns (customer, product, order), attributes are their properties (email, price), relationships are the verbs (a customer places an order), and constraints are the rules (quantity must be positive). /DataModelingForDataEngineers/.h: 1.4 Identity management: primary keys, foreign keys, and alternate keys
/DataModelingForDataEngineers/.t: In plain terms. A key is how you point at exactly one thing. Your passport number is a business key, issued by someone else. The seat number on your boarding pass is closer to a surrogate key, assigned by the airline for this one trip. Primary key. Identifies one row in a relation. It is unique and non-null. Example: (order_id, line_number) on an order line. Foreign key. References a candidate key

In plain terms. Cardinality answers “how many?” and modality answers “is it required?” A customer can have zero or many orders; an order must have exactly one customer. Cardinality describes how many instances can participate in a relationship. Modality (also called optionality or minimum cardinality) describes whether participation is optional or required. /DataModelingForDataEngineers/.t: In plain terms. A spreadsheet is structured, a JSON API response is semi-structured, and a scanned invoice PDF is unstructured. The less structure the data has, the more of its model you must add yourself. These terms describe how much organization is represented in the data, not whether it is important or valuable. Structured data has named fields with stable types and relationships. Model it by

A data model is the agreed meaning of each dataset: what one row represents, which keys identify it, which time its attributes describe, and how its measures may be aggregated. Data engineers own the pipelines that create those rows, so they are the ones who either preserve that meaning or break it with a bad join, a blind append, or an untyped column. /DataModelingForDataEngineers/.t: In plain terms. Normalization means storing each fact in exactly one place. If a city name is written on every order, renaming the city means editing thousands of rows, and missing one leaves the data contradicting itself. Normalization organizes a relational model to reduce update anomalies and inconsistent repetition. The normal forms are tests against a logical schema, not a contest to reach th

Each row-column position holds one value from the column’s domain, and repeating groups become related rows. It prevents columns such as phone_1 , phone_2 and phone_3 , which break the day a customer adds a fourth phone.

The table is in 1NF, and every non-key attribute depends on the whole candidate key, not on part of it. It prevents a product name repeated on every (order_id, line_number) row when the name depends only on product_id .
The table is in 2NF, and no non-key attribute depends on the key through another non-key attribute. It prevents customer_id -> postal_code -> city from being stored redundantly on every order.

For every nontrivial functional dependency X -> Y , X is a superkey. It catches determinants that are not candidate keys, which a schema can still have while meeting 3NF. /DataModelingForDataEngineers/.t: In plain terms. A fact table records things that happened and can be counted or summed: an order line with its quantity and amount. Dimension tables describe the who, what, where and when you filter and group by: customer, product, date. Questions such as “revenue by product category by month” read as facts sliced by dimensions. /DataModelingForDataEngineers/.h: 3.1 Slowly Changing Dimensions (SCD Types 0–6 Deep Dive)
/DataModelingForDataEngineers/.t: In plain terms. Customers move, products get renamed, sales reps change territory. An SCD type is the rule for what happens to history when a dimension attribute changes: forget the old value, keep it in a new row, or keep it in an extra column. The SCD number is a response policy for changed attributes, not a property of the whole dimension table. Apply policies at the attribute level. Type 2 is
The first accepted value never changes. Use it when the original value is durable by definition, or explicitly labeled “original”, such as original_signup_channel .
Only the latest value is kept. Use it to correct an error, or when the business intentionally restates all history with the new value.

Each effective version gets its own row and its own surrogate key. Use it when historical facts must resolve to the attribute version that was valid at event time. This is the type interviews ask about most.
The row keeps the current value plus one or a few prior values in extra columns. Use it when a limited comparison, such as current region versus previous region, is enough.
Volatile attributes move to a separate dimension of attribute profiles. Use it when several attributes change rapidly, or their combinations would explode the base dimension.

/DataModelingForDataEngineers/.t: The model sits inside a platform and an organization. Processing topology decides how results are refreshed; ownership decides who defines and supports the contract; metadata makes its meaning and dependencies discoverable. None of these choices replaces the need to define a correct row grain.

/DataModelingForDataEngineers/.h: 4.1 Data processing topologies: Lambda architecture vs. Kappa architecture
/DataModelingForDataEngineers/.t: In plain terms. Lambda runs two pipelines, a slow, complete batch one and a fast, approximate streaming one, and merges their answers. Kappa runs one streaming pipeline and, when the logic changes, replays the stored event log through the new version. Both patterns address the tension between low-latency updates and the ability to recompute results after code or business rules change.

/DataModelingForDataEngineers/.h: Lambda architecture: two paths, merged at read time
/DataModelingForDataEngineers/.t: Nathan Marz described Lambda around one idea: keep an immutable master dataset, and treat every view as a function of it that can be recomputed. Batch recomputation is complete and correct but slow, so a second, faster path covers the hours the batch has not reached yet. Step by step: Every event is appended to the master dataset and, at the same time, delivered to the speed layer. The batch layer

Jay Kreps proposed Kappa in Questioning the Lambda Architecture as a response to that duplication: if the stream processor can reprocess history, there is no need for a separate batch system. Step by step: All events go to one log, retained long enough to cover the longest rebuild window. /DataModelingForDataEngineers/.h: 5.1 Indexing mechanics: B-trees, bitmaps, hash, clustered vs. non-clustered
/DataModelingForDataEngineers/.t: In plain terms. An index is the index at the back of a book: instead of reading every page to find “Iceberg”, you look it up and jump to page 212. It speeds up reads, but every new page added to the book means updating the index too. An index is an access structure that helps an engine find rows without examining every data page. Its useful operators depend on the index type and engine.
Fits equality, ranges, and ordered scans on sortable values. It adds write amplification and storage, and a low-selectivity predicate may still scan the table.
Fits equality lookups in engines that support hash indexes. It cannot serve a range or an ordered scan.
Fits low-cardinality analytic predicates in engines that implement bitmap indexes. Update and concurrency behavior are engine-specific, so it is not a general OLTP index.
Fit membership tests on arrays, tokens, and other multi-valued structures. Index size and update cost can be high, and the supported operators depend on the engine.

Fit large ranges that are physically correlated with the column, such as append-ordered timestamps. The summaries are coarse, so they return false-positive blocks that still need filtering. /DataModelingForDataEngineers/.h: 5.3 Key considerations for designing scalable database systems
/DataModelingForDataEngineers/.t: Choose keys for identity and distribution separately. A sequential surrogate can be an effective dimension key but a hotspot for a distributed write path; a random UUID may spread writes while increasing key size and reducing locality. Avoid hot partitions. Tenant, date, or status keys can be extremely skewed. Measure the distribution before choosing a partition key, shard count, or hash strategy.

In plain terms. Partitioning splits one table into folders, such as one per day, so a query for one day opens one folder. Sharding splits data across separate database servers. /WhyIcebergExists/.h: The Hive table is a directory
/WhyIcebergExists/.t: For a decade the answer to “what is a table on a data lake” was: a directory, plus a row in a metastore saying where that directory is and what columns to expect. Everything good about that design comes from its simplicity: any engine that can list a path and read Parquet can read the table. Everything bad comes from the same place — the set of files in the table is whatever happens to be in the d

Iceberg replaces “the files in this directory” with “the files this metadata says are in the table”. That is the whole idea, and everything else is a consequence. The catalog holds one pointer: which metadata file is current. A commit writes new metadata and swaps that pointer atomically. The swap is the commit — before it, readers see the old table; after it, the new one; never anything in betwee
These are not separate features bolted on. Each one falls out of tracking files in metadata.

Every commit writes a new metadata file rather than editing the old one. A table created and appended to three times accumulates them predictably: Three metadata files per commit: a manifest, a manifest list, and a new metadata.json . Old snapshots stay valid because their metadata still exists and still names its files, which is exactly what time travel reads.

/WhyIcebergExists/.h: Schema changes that touch no data
/WhyIcebergExists/.t: Adding a column, renaming one and changing a type, on a table holding 9,000 rows: Three data files before, three after. The rename was a metadata edit. It is safe because Iceberg identifies columns by field id , not by name or position: amount became amount_usd and kept id 4 . The Parquet files still record field 4; the schema now calls it something else. This is the fix for the Hive failure where

A table partitioned by month, switched to day, then appended to: Two files still carry spec_id = 0 . Nothing was rewritten, both layouts coexist on disk, and all rows stay queryable through one table. In a Hive table the partition layout is the directory structure, so changing it means moving every file. Partitioning is also hidden : the query names the real column and Iceberg applies the transfor

/WhyIcebergExists/.h: Seeing the difference in one session
/WhyIcebergExists/.t: The argument is short enough to run. Both tables hold the same rows; only the format differs. Now ask each one a question only the Iceberg table can answer: There is no equivalent for the Hive table, and that is the whole difference stated as a capability rather than an argument: the Iceberg table knows what it is made of.

Four concrete situations, each routine on a directory-based table. A reader sees a half-written partition. A job overwrites dt=2026-01-06 by deleting and rewriting files; a query running at that moment reads whatever exists. On Iceberg the query resolved a snapshot before the write began and is unaffected. Two writers both “succeed”. Two jobs write to the same partition concurrently and the result

Being fair about the other side of the ledger. Three jobs you did not have before. Compaction, delete-file compaction and snapshot expiry. None is optional on a table under real write traffic, and a table that skips them degrades in ways a Hive table does not. A catalog to operate. Something must own the pointer and swap it atomically. That is a service to deploy, secure, monitor and back up — inf

Iceberg is not free, and pretending otherwise sets people up for surprises. Metadata is a thing you now operate. Every commit writes files. Streaming writes accumulate them quickly, and tables need compaction, snapshot expiry and occasionally manifest rewriting on a schedule. Every engine needs Iceberg support. A Hive table can be read by anything that lists a directory. An Iceberg table needs a r

/WhyIcebergExists/.h: When the older design is still right
/WhyIcebergExists/.t: A table written once and read as a whole, small enough that listing is instant, consumed by one engine, with no update or delete requirement and no need for history — that is a directory of Parquet files, and adding a table format to it buys complexity rather than capability. The moment any of those stops being true — concurrent writers, row-level deletes, a schema that changes, an auditor asking

A Hive table says “the data is over there”. An Iceberg table says “these exact files, with this schema, as of this snapshot”. Every Iceberg feature people list separately — ACID, time travel, schema evolution, partition evolution, hidden partitioning — is that one sentence applied to a different problem. Which is also why they compose: they are not features, they are consequences.

The project has been going since late 2016, and the docs list Uber, Amazon, ByteDance and Robinhood among the organisation

/ApacheHudiGuide/.h: What problem was it built for?
/ApacheHudiGuide/.t: The architecture Hudi replaced was Parquet files in partitioned directories with a Hive Metastore on top. Four failures drove its design, and each has a symptom you may have hit. Updating one record meant rewriting a partition. With immutable files and no record identity, correcting a single row means reading the partition, merging, and writing it back. A change stream delivering a few thousand up
Almost everything in Hudi is built from four things. Learn these and the rest of the system reads as composition.

A Hudi table declares a record key , the column or columns that identify a record. It is not optional in the way a primary key is optional in a plain Parquet table: it is part of the table contract, and it is what makes an update addressable. Alongside it sits an ordering field , used to decide which version of a record wins when two arrive for the same key. On the 1.x line the SQL property is ord

The timeline is Hudi’s record of everything that has happened to the table. Each entry is an instant : an action, a time, and a state. In 1.x the timeline lives in its own directory, since hoodie.timeline.path defaults to timeline and hoodie.timeline.history.path to history . An instant moves through three states, and the filename changes with each: Readers only ever see the completed form, which

Data is organised into file groups , each identified by a file ID that never changes. A record key, once assigned to a file group, stays there. A file slice is one version of a group: a base file plus any log files written against it. This is the unit that makes an update local. Without it, “update this record” has to be answered against the whole table; with it, the question becomes “which file g

The index maps a record key to the file group holding it. This is the piece with no equivalent in the other major table formats, and it is why Hudi behaves differently on write-heavy workloads. hoodie.index.type has no default value of its own. The Spark and Java clients fall back to SIMPLE and Flink to INMEMORY , chosen in code rather than in the config, so a writer that never sets it is running

/ApacheHudiGuide/.h: Architecture: what does a table look like on disk?
/ApacheHudiGuide/.t: Those four primitives produce a specific on-disk shape. A Merge-on-Read table, partitioned by city: Note that log files begin with a dot, so a plain listing hides them. A Merge-on-Read partition can look deceptively like Copy-on-Write at a glance.

The index lookup is the step that distinguishes Hudi. On a table format without record identity, the equivalent step is a join between the incoming batch and the table, whose cost scales with how much of the table the join has to touch. With an index, it is a lookup whose cost scales with the batch. On a small batch against a large table, that is the whole difference.

Reading is a reconciliation, and Hudi lets you choose how much reconciliation you want. The three query types come from DataSourceReadOptions : Query type Reads On Copy-on-Write On Merge-on-Read snapshot (default) Latest committed state Base files Base files merged with log files read_optimized Base files only Same as snapshot State as of the last compaction incremental Records changed between two

/ApacheHudiGuide/.h: What does it look like end to end?
/ApacheHudiGuide/.t: One schema throughout: ride events arriving as a change stream, keyed by trip_id , partitioned by city_id , ordered by updated_at . Every statement below is literal, with the rows written inline, so you can paste the whole section into a shell and watch a real table take shape on local disk. Everything runs in one spark-sql session. Hudi’s Spark SQL surface covers DDL, upserts, incremental reads a

Two small conventions there are worth copying. The partition column is declared last, which is how Hudi’s own DDL examples are written, and the INSERT names its columns rather than relying on position. Together they mean you never have to work out whether the table’s column order is the order you typed. Three rows, two partitions. Because the table declared trip_id as its primary key, those keys a

The interesting batch is one that mixes an update, a correction that arrived late, and a brand new trip. Writing it inline makes the ordering rule visible: Read the result rather than trusting the statement. trip-1001 takes the new fare because its updated_at moved forward. trip-1002 keeps 11.75 , because the incoming row carries an older updated_at and the table was created with recordMergeMode =

The current release registers table-valued functions, so an incremental read is ordinary SQL. hudi_table_changes takes the table, a format of latest_state or cdc , a start instant, and optionally an end instant: Two companion functions are worth knowing. hudi_query picks a query type without a read option, and hudi_metadata exposes the metadata table as a queryable relation:

The data still exists in older file slices until cleaning removes them. For a right-to-erasure obligation the delete is not complete until retention has expired those slices, so the cleaner is part of the compliance story rather than just housekeeping.

Before the parts that are distinctive, here is the baseline. These are the capabilities a Hudi table has because it is a modern table format, and they are what you are adopting whichever one you pick. Feature What it means on a Hudi table ACID transactions Writes commit atomically as a completed instant on the timeline. A half-finished write is .inflight and invisible to queries Snapshot isolation

Everything in the table above, every table format now offers in some form, which is why a feature checklist is a poor way to choose between them. The eight capabilities below are the ones that are either unique to Hudi or materially further along here than elsewhere, and each maps to a workload where the difference shows up. Capability What it replaces Where you feel it Record-level index A join t

No other major table format maps a record key to the file that holds it. Iceberg and Delta describe a table as a set of files; neither has a notion of “the row with this key”, so an update is planned as a join. Hudi’s index turns that into a lookup. The record index comes in two scopes, GLOBAL_RECORD_LEVEL_INDEX for keys unique table-wide and RECORD_LEVEL_INDEX for keys unique within a partition,

/ApacheHudiGuide/.h: 2. A multi-modal index, not just a file listing
/ApacheHudiGuide/.t: The metadata table at .hoodie/metadata is an internal Hudi table, and it holds seven kinds of index, each in its own partition: Partition Holds files Partition to file listing, so planning does not list object storage column_stats Per-column min/max per file, for data skipping partition_stats Column statistics aggregated per partition bloom_filters Bloom filters for BLOOM index lookups record_inde

/ApacheHudiGuide/.h: 3. Incremental queries as a first-class read mode
/ApacheHudiGuide/.t: hoodie.datasource.query.type = incremental returns the records that changed between two instants. This is not a change-data-feed bolted on later; it is one of the three query types the format was designed around, and it is why Hudi is often the source of a chained pipeline where each stage consumes only its upstream’s changes.

Most table formats have one concurrency story. Hudi documents four, because it draws a line between three kinds of process that touch a table: writers that issue write operations, table services that rewrite data or metadata for optimisation and bookkeeping, and readers that run queries. Different pairs of those get different mechanisms. Control Governs What it gives you Snapshot isolation Writers

Hudi ships the maintenance as part of the platform rather than as procedures you remember to call, and each can run inline with writes or asynchronously: Service Does Timeline action Compaction Merges log files into a new base file compaction Log compaction Merges log blocks without rewriting the base file logcompaction Clustering Reorganises layout, sorting and file sizing clustering Cleaning Rem

savepoint marks a state and protects it from cleaning; restore returns the table to it. Together they are a point-in-time recovery mechanism at the table level, which is a different guarantee from time travel: time travel lets you read an old state, restore makes it current again.

/ApacheHudiGuide/.h: 7. Write operations beyond insert and upsert
/ApacheHudiGuide/.t: WriteOperationType includes INSERT , UPSERT , BULK_INSERT , DELETE , BOOTSTRAP , INSERT_OVERWRITE , INSERT_OVERWRITE_TABLE , DELETE_PARTITION , BUCKET_RESCALE , CLUSTER , COMPACT , LOG_COMPACT , INDEX and ALTER_SCHEMA . BOOTSTRAP deserves a mention: it turns an existing Parquet dataset into a Hudi table by generating metadata that points at the existing files, rather than rewriting terabytes to ad

The project ships a managed ingestion utility, HoodieStreamer in hudi-utilities , which reads from a source, applies transformations and writes a Hudi table with checkpointing and schema handling built in. Most table formats leave ingestion entirely to you.

/ApacheHudiGuide/.h: Which engines can read and write it?
/ApacheHudiGuide/.t: Engine Snapshot Read-optimized Incremental Writes Spark Yes Yes Yes Yes Flink Yes Yes Yes Yes Trino Yes Yes Through the connector No Presto Yes Yes Through the connector No Hive Yes Yes Limited No Writes are a Spark and Flink story; the other engines read. If your ingestion is neither Spark nor Flink, that is worth confirming before adopting Hudi.

/ApacheHudiGuide/.h: When does a simpler choice win?
/ApacheHudiGuide/.t: Hudi’s design assumes records have identity and change over time. Where that assumption holds, everything above earns its keep. Where it does not, there are good simpler answers, and recognising them is part of using the tool well. Append-only tables need no index and no merge. bulk_insert skips tagging entirely, and if you never correct a row, plain partitioned Parquet is less machinery with fewe

Set hoodie.index.type explicitly. An absent value still resolves to SIMPLE on Spark, whose cost scales with table size rather than batch size. Choose the index scope from your data model. Global versus partition-scoped changes correctness when partition values mutate, not just speed. Use EVENT_TIME_ORDERING when late-arriving corrections must not overwrite newer values. Decide who runs compaction

Do I have to use Merge-on-Read? No, and it is not the default. hoodie.datasource.write.table.type defaults to Copy-on-Write, which is the right choice for most tables written a few times a day. Merge-on-Read is the option you reach for when writes are frequent and someone will own compaction. What if my data has no natural primary key? Hudi can build one. hoodie.datasource.write.keygenerator.class

Back to the configuration that looks like overhead on day one. The record key, the table type and the compaction job are not accessories bolted onto a table format — each one is a place where Hudi’s founding assumption, that a record has an identity, stops being an idea and becomes something you configure. Nearly every feature in this post traces back to that assumption, which is the argument Apac

The published parquet-cli runtime jar deliberately does not bundle Hadoop, which keeps it small and lets it pick up whatever Hadoop and connector versions your cluster already has. There are two easy ways to run it.

Every example from here on uses that parquet wrapper.

schema gives you the Avro view, which is what most downstream readers see: The Parquet message type is a different thing, and when you are debugging a type-mismatch it is the one you want, because it shows physical types, required versus optional , and the logical-type annotations. It reports the writer, the key-value metadata, the Parquet message type, and per-column statistics per row group: Four things to read off this, in the order they usually matter: Created by identifies the writer. A Parquet file is a sequence of row groups , each a horizontal slice of the rows. Within a row group, each column’s values for those rows live in one column chunk , which is the unit that gets its own encoding, compression and min/max statistics. A column chunk

Its own help text is explicit that prune is deprecated and will be removed in 2.0.0 in favour of it. Merging several files and switching the codec at the same time:

Here is the behaviour worth understanding before you rely on it. Reading the merged file back: Two 10-row inputs became one file with two row groups of 10 rows rather than one row group of 20. rewrite copies row groups intact, which is exactly why it is fast: it moves column chunks without decoding them. That makes it ideal for changing a codec, dropping a column or consolidating a handful of file

When you prune a column, it is worth knowing which command to verify with. Prune a column and nullify another: The Parquet message type is correctly pruned to seven columns: The parquet.avro.schema entry in the file’s key-value metadata still declares phone_number , because rewrite copies key-value metadata through untouched. An Avro-model reader follows that schema, finds no column, and returns n

Nullify needs somewhere to put the null, so it applies to optional columns. On a required column it stops and tells you clearly: To scrub a non-nullable column, prune it instead, or rewrite the data through an engine that can change required to optional first.

Each tier answers one question. The catalog: which metadata file is current? The metadata tier: which data files are in the table, and what is in them? The data tier: the rows. Almost every operational question resolves to “which tier is this?” — and the answer determines the fix.

One pointer, swapped atomically. That is the whole tier, and its smallness is the point: the less it does, the easier it is to make correct. It is also the only tier that cannot be rebuilt from the others. Lose the data and you have lost rows; lose the metadata and you have lost history; lose the catalog and you have lost which metadata file was current — which, with a directory full of metadata.j

The table’s state: current schema and every past schema, every partition spec, the snapshot list, table properties, and the pointer to each snapshot’s manifest list. One is written per commit, never edited. Schemas are kept plurally because old snapshots were written under old schemas, and time travel has to read them correctly.

One per snapshot, an Avro file naming the manifests that make up that snapshot — with a summary of each, including its partition range: Those summaries let a planner discard an entire manifest — and every file in it — without opening it. This level is also what makes snapshots cheap: a new manifest list points at unchanged manifests from the previous snapshot rather than copying them, so successiv

The leaf level, listing data files with statistics: Record count, partition value, and per-column min/max keyed by field id . This is where metadata stops being bookkeeping and becomes a query accelerator: a filter that cannot match a file’s bounds skips the file unopened. Each manifest also records the spec_id its files were written under, which is what lets partition layouts change without rewri

Parquet (or ORC or Avro) holding rows, plus delete files on v2 and later marking rows removed without rewriting. Nothing here is Iceberg-specific — the Parquet is ordinary Parquet. The table format is entirely the tiers above it, which is why migrating a Hive table is a metadata operation and why any engine can read the data once told which files to read.

A table with 5,000 rows written once, listed from object storage: Five objects: one data, four metadata. Two metadata.json because there were two commits — the create and the append. And the growth rate, across three appends to a partitioned table: Three metadata files per commit , regardless of how many rows it carried. For a streaming table this is the number that matters: metadata grows with co

Every tier is queryable, which makes “which tier is my problem in” a question you answer rather than guess. That last query is the single most useful one on a production table. content is 0 for data, 1 for position deletes and 2 for equality deletes, so one row tells you whether you have a small-file problem, a delete-accumulation problem, or neither.

Resource allocation. Prefer several medium executors over a few very large ones. A large heap makes garbage collection pauses longer, and an executor with many cores contends on the same memory pool. Executors in the range of four to five cores are a common starting point, with memory sized so that cores × per-task working set fits. Data locality. “Avoid regex” is common advice and too blunt to act on. What the implementation actually does: Spark compiles the pattern once when the pattern expression is foldable — a literal — and caches it. When the pattern is not foldable, such as a pattern coming from another column, it is compiled per row . So a literal regex is not the disaster the advice implies. /SparkReleaseHistory/.t: Spark has had one durable architectural habit: each era moves the thing you program against one level further from the machine, and one level closer to a description of intent. Each move buys something and costs something: The 1.x RDD era: you describe the computation You program against an RDD of ordinary JVM or Python objects, and you pass functions to map , filter and reduceByKey . /SparkReleaseHistory/.t: Reading releases one at a time hides the fact that most features arrive in stages. A capability is introduced as experimental, becomes usable a release or two later, and becomes a default a release or two after that. Five of those threads run across the whole history, and placing a feature on its thread tells you whether it is experimental, usable or finished. Python performance It started with ro

Spark was written at UC Berkeley’s AMPLab and open-sourced in 2010. The public releases before 1.0 are worth knowing about for one reason: they set down every primitive the 1.x line then built on. The RDD, lineage-based recovery, the shell, caching and the first three language bindings were all in place before anything was declared stable. In this section and every release section below, each feat

The first line’s job was to turn a fast research engine into something an operations team would accept, and then to discover that the RDD was the wrong abstraction for most of the work people were doing with it. Read the 1.x features in two groups: 1.0 to 1.2 make Spark operable (submission, security, monitoring, a shuffle that scales), and 1.3 to 1.6 replace the RDD with the DataFrame and rebuild

The release that made Spark deployable rather than merely usable. spark-submit One submission path for local, Standalone, Mesos and YARN; before this, each cluster manager had its own launch story. How it works. The theory behind it is the split between the driver , which holds the SparkContext , builds the DAG of stages and schedules tasks, and the executors , which run those tasks and hold cache

Sort-based shuffle, available A new shuffle writer, opt-in here and the default from 1.2. How it works. A shuffle moves data so that all records with the same key end up in the same partition. The map side of a shuffle writes each task’s output grouped by destination partition; the reduce side fetches its slice from every map task. The sort writer buffers records in memory tagged with their destin

The release that changed the most defaults in the shortest note. Sort shuffle becomes the default spark.shuffle.manager changed from hash to sort , the single most consequential default flip in Spark’s history. How it works. The release where Spark stopped being an RDD engine. The DataFrame API Named, typed columns in Python, Scala and Java. This is the oldest API in the post that still runs unchanged today: How it works. A DataFrame is not data. It is an immutable, lazily built logical plan: every transformation ( select , where , groupBy ) returns a new DataFrame whose plan has one more node, and nothing runs until

Like PySpark, SparkR runs your R code in an R process that drives a JVM through a socket; DataFrame operations are translated into JVM calls, so they run at the same speed as from Scala, while R functions passed to dapply or gapply run in R worker processes on the executors. Good to know: SparkR was deprecated in 4.0 and is still presen

Tungsten’s main release. The theme is that the JVM’s object model is the bottleneck, so Spark should stop using it for data. Code generation on by default Almost all DataFrame and SQL functions were compiled to bytecode instead of interpreted. How it works. See the 1.1 entry on dynamic bytecode generation: the expression tree becomes one generated function per projection or filter, with primitive

A Spark application has exactly one SparkContext , which owns the connection to the cluster manager, the executors and the scheduler. A SparkSession sits on top of it and owns the SQL side: the SQL configuration, the catalog, temporary views and registered functions.

A record’s event time , when it happened, can be well behind its processing time , when Spark sees it, because of network delays, offline devices or retries. /SparkReleaseHistory/.t: The 2.x engine made one plan from estimates and executed it. The estimates were frequently wrong, because nobody knows the selectivity of a filter over data nobody has read yet. The 3.x line’s theme is letting the engine revise itself, and separately, admitting that Python is the primary language. AQE runs the stages that have no dependencies first, and when a stage finishes it has something the planner never had before: the actual size of every shuffle partition it wrote. In a classic Spark application the driver runs inside the client process. That design made Spark easy to start with and hard to operate at scale, for five reasons that all come from the same coupling: Every client is a full driver. How it works. The client does not know what a table is, cannot resolve a column, and never optimises anything. When you write DataFrame code, each call only adds a node to an unresolved logical plan , a tree of relations and expressions that refers to tables and columns by name, encoded as a protocol buffer . /StructuredStreamingInternals/.h: What is actually hard about streaming?
/StructuredStreamingInternals/.t: Restarting a batch job is free. It reads its input, writes its output, and if it died halfway you run it again. A streaming query has no such luxury: it has consumed input that will not be replayed by default, it has emitted output that downstream systems have already seen, and it holds aggregates in memory that took hours to accumulate. A restart has to resume, not repeat. Structured Streaming so

You should have written a Structured Streaming query and know what a trigger, a source and a sink are. The loop is the same for every source and sink. The write-ahead order is the whole trick. offsets/<batchId> is durable before any processing starts, so a crash mid-batch leaves an offset entry with no matching commit entry. “Structured Streaming processes records one at a time.” It runs micro-batches. Continuous processing exists as a separate, limited execution mode; the default and the one described here is a loop of small batches. “The checkpoint stores my data.” It stores offsets, watermarks, configuration and state. The input data is not in there, which is why a source that cannot replay a range breaks recovery.

A streaming query is a loop that writes its intent, does the work, then writes its completion. offsets/ is the intent, commits/ is the completion, and the difference between them after a crash is the recovery plan. /TableMaintenance/.t: A lakehouse table is append-structured. A write does not modify existing files; it adds new ones and records, in metadata, which files now constitute the table. The maintenance vocabulary differs because the storage models differ. In Iceberg, a snapshot points at a manifest list, which points at manifests, which list data files. In Hudi, records are grouped into file groups; each slice holds a base file and, for Merge-on-Read tables, log files carrying updates that have not yet been merged in.

“Interoperability means the data is copied.” The Parquet files are shared. Maintenance that depends on someone remembering is maintenance that stops. The shape that works: Two operational notes. remove_orphan_files deletes files no snapshot references, and a file being written right now looks exactly like an orphan — use an age threshold of days, and never run it while a long write is in flight. And maintenance jobs are writers : they commit, they can conflict with your

“Target file size guarantees file size.” The measured write produced 124,966 and 496,738 bytes against a 1 MiB target. “Compaction is maintenance.” It is one of three jobs, and the only one that reclaims storage is expiry. “Object storage mode is just a layout preference.” It is the fix for prefix throttling, and it changes the failure mode under concurrency. “Expiring snapshots is cleanup.” It is

An Iceberg table has two clocks. One counts data files and delete files, and compaction resets it. The other counts snapshots, manifests and metadata files, and expiry and manifest rewriting reset it. Production operation is keeping both wound, choosing a catalog that can commit safely, and setting the layout properties before the first write rather than after the first incident.

/HudiIncrementalProcessing/.t: Every write to a Hudi table produces an instant on the timeline, under .hoodie/ . An incremental read is then a filter over that timeline: give me the records touched by instants in this range. In Hudi 1.x the timeline files carry two timestamps, and the filename says so: The first number is when the write started ; the second is when it completed . /HudiIncrementalProcessing/.h: How far back can you read?
/HudiIncrementalProcessing/.t: Only as far as the timeline goes, and the timeline is deliberately bounded by two services that exist to keep it that way: Cleaning removes old file versions. Once the versions an instant referred to are gone, that instant cannot be served incrementally. Archival moves old instants out of the active timeline entirely. So an incremental checkpoint is perishable. A pipeline that stops for longer tha

Both support incremental reads and the semantics above are identical. What differs is where the changed records are read from: on copy-on-write the reader picks up new base files, on merge-on-read it must also read log files for instants not yet compacted. The practical consequence is that on a merge-on-read table, an incremental read competes with compaction for the same state, and a read spannin

“An incremental read gives me a change log.” It gives you the latest state of changed records. No before images, no per-change rows, and no deletes. “I can turn CDC on when I need it.” It is a table-creation property. Does an incremental read see a record that was inserted and then deleted inside the range? No. There is no latest state to return, so it is absent — and indistinguishable from a record that never existed. CDC mode shows

The incremental read is the capability Hudi is named for, and it does what it says as long as you know what “what changed” means here: the current value of touched records, with deletes absent and history collapsed. When that is not enough, CDC is a different query type with a different schema and a decision you must have made at table creation. The part worth carrying away is the timestamp. Hudi

/KerberoSetup/.h: Install & Configure Kerberos Server & Client in Linux
/KerberoSetup/.t: Let’s see how we can install, setup and configure Kerberos in a Cluster. We will install Kerberos Server in one machine and Kerberos client in rest of the machines.
We need to install the Kerberos client on every node in the cluster. On RHEL 7 and older, yum replaces dnf . On Debian and Ubuntu the client package is krb5-user instead.

The Kerberos server usually goes on the master node, though that is a convention rather than a rule; any server in the cluster will do. On Debian and Ubuntu the equivalents are krb5-kdc and krb5-admin-server , and their configuration lives in a different directory, so follow the Ubuntu server guide linked at the end for those paths.
The configuration lives in two files, one for the KDC and one for clients.
Login Kerberos Server Installed machine $ vi /var/kerberos/krb5kdc/kdc.conf In the above kdc.conf file we choosed realm is EXAMPLE.COM

Create the KDC (Key Distribution Centre) database that the Kerberos server runs on. $ kdb5_util -r EXAMPLE.COM create -s It prompts for a master password. Note it down: every later KDC database operation, including a restart, needs it.
$ vi /var/kerberos/krb5kdc/kadm5.acl Set your realm name. For this walkthrough: */admin@EXAMPLE.COM *

Note this Step MUST BE Executed only in the KDC Server machine – NOT in any Kerberos client machines. $ kadmin.local This will bring you to kadmin.local prompt. In that prompt, use the highlighted command. Note you have to use your own Realm name. kadmin.local: addprinc root/admin@EXAMPLE.COM To see list of all principals created – kadmin.local : listprincs

/KerberoSetup/.h: Step 7: Restart the Kerberos Admin & KDC Server
/KerberoSetup/.t: Note these steps MUST be done in KDC Server machine. Start both services and enable them so the KDC comes back after a reboot: Confirm both came up before moving on: We are done with the Setup. We will test it from Kerberos as well Client servers.

Test the Kerberos installation. Use the below command – Check if any Ticket exists $ klist If no tickets exist in the cache, create a new one $ kinit root/admin Check again if you have any ticket $ klist Hopefully now you can see tickets listed here. If you want to destroy any ticket, use $ kdestroy

/KerberoSetup/.h: Testing 2: Test Kerberos from the client machine
/KerberoSetup/.t: In previous step, we tested Kerberos from Kerberos server itself. Now test from the client machine, which is where users actually authenticate before reaching a service on the network.

Use a non-admin user. Run these on the KDC server to create one. $ kadmin.local In kadmin.local prompt use – kadmin.local: addprinc rangareddy@EXAMPLE.COM so we have created a normal user rangareddy .

/KerberoSetup/.h: 2. Create a keytab file for the user
/KerberoSetup/.t: We will create a keytab file for the user rangareddy $ kadmin.local In kadmin.local prompt, use below kadmin.local: xst -norandkey -k /tmp/rangareddy.keytab rangareddy@EXAMPLE.COM It will create a keytab file rangareddy.keytab in /tmp directory for the rangareddy.

In previous step, we created the rangareddy.keytab file in KDC SERVER machine. Copy the keytab file to the client machine. Lets place it in /root/rangareddy.keytab in client machine. Now in the client machine, open command prompt Create a kerberos ticket $ kinit -kt /root/rangareddy.keytab rangareddy@EXAMPLE.COM Check if ticket created $ klist
